query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: compare the load-bearing integrity and caloric performance of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy with and without the hierarchical microstructure under applied-field and pressure-field operation

cited_evidence.text: However, there is also a question of the role of high configurational entropy in these materials with respect to properties, particularly how such high-entropy alloys compare with other equiatomic multi-element systems. Here we examine a variant of the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy in which two of the elements have been removed. The resulting CrCoNi alloy, an equiatomic ‘medium-entropy alloy' (MEA), has a single-phase, fcc crystal structure, whose uniaxial tensile properties have recently been reported. The experimental results (X-ray diffraction and backscattered electron, BSE, images) are consistent with the CrCoNi ternary phase diagrams, which indicate that the equiatomic composition is a single-phase solid solution at elevated temperatures. (XRD and BSE analyses of the five-component CrMnFeCoNi alloy after casting and homogenization showed that it too is single-phase fcc and remains so after recrystallization when examined by transmission electron microscopy. Strength and ductility (and hence toughness) are key mechanical properties of structural materials, although these properties are often mutually exclusive. In crystalline metallic materials, strength and ductility depend on the presence of crystal defects and how they move under mechanical loading. Dislocations serve as the prime carrier of plasticity in metals and their motion to create plastic deformation is strongly influenced by interactions with other dislocations as well as defects such as solute atoms, stacking faults, grain boundaries (GBs) and reinforcement particles or precipitates. In general, strong interactions (obstacles) strengthen a material although this often limits its ability to plastically deform. Twinning, however, appears to be a deformation mechanism capable of defeating this ‘conflict' between strength and ductility. The presence of twins usually serves to impede dislocation motion and induce strengthening, but multiple twinning systems can also enhance ductility.
